markup-vs-margin.formula: markup% = (price-cost)/cost*100; margin% = (price-cost)/price*100; margin% = markup%/(1+markup%); markup% = margin%/(1-margin%); price = cost*(1+markup%) = cost/(1-margin%).
markup-vs-margin.edition: Standard managerial-accounting pricing identity (cost-volume-profit), universal public formula; AICPA / introductory managerial-accounting texts, by name.
markup-vs-margin.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
markup-vs-margin.editionNote: Markup and margin diverge sharply (50% markup = 33.3% margin); margin >= 100% is guarded (price would be infinite).

assumptions.name: Two-of-four
assumptions.value: any two of cost, price, markup, or margin resolve the rest

flocculator-paddle-power.formula: v_tip = 2 x pi x paddle_radius_ft x wheel_rpm / 60; v_rel = v_tip x (1 - slip_factor); power_ftlbs = 0.5 x drag_coeff x 1.937 x paddle_area_ft2 x v_rel^3; power_w = power_ftlbs x 1.35582; power_hp = power_ftlbs / 550.
flocculator-paddle-power.edition: Camp paddle flocculator power (water-treatment design practice), by name.
flocculator-paddle-power.freeAccess: The Camp paddle-power drag relation is public water-treatment design material; the flocculator design and the operator govern.
flocculator-paddle-power.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
flocculator-paddle-power.editionNote: The power goes as the CUBE of the relative velocity, so a small speed change swings it hard. The water slips (it rotates with the paddles) so the relative velocity is only (1 - k) of the tip speed - ignoring the slip overstates the power by 1/(1 - k)^3, about 2.4x at k = 0.25 and 4.6x at k = 0.40. The drag coefficient (about 1.8, 1.0 to 1.8 reported) and the slip factor (about 0.25, 0.25 to 0.40 reported) are user inputs because the references disagree; the drag physics is exact once they are chosen. This power feeds flocculation-g-value for the mixing gradient. The flocculator design and the operator govern - a design aid, not a metered power.

assumptions.name: Cube law and slip
assumptions.value: P scales with v_rel^3, and v_rel = (1 - k) x tip speed; ignoring the slip overstates the power by 1/(1 - k)^3, about 2.4x at k = 0.25 and 4.6x at k = 0.40

assumptions.name: User-chosen constants
assumptions.value: Cd (about 1.8, 1.0-1.8 reported) and k (about 0.25, 0.25-0.40 reported) are inputs because the references disagree

solar-egc-690-45.formula: basis = OCPD rating > 0 ? OCPD : 1.25 x PV Isc; EGC = Table 250.122 size for the basis, never smaller than 14 AWG; the 250.122(B) proportional upsize does not apply (690.45).
solar-egc-690-45.edition: The NEC 2023 690.45 equipment grounding conductors for PV systems, with Table 250.122, by name.
solar-egc-690-45.freeAccess: The NEC is available through NFPA's free online read-only access at nfpa.org; the 690.45 and Table 250.122 provisions are in the published code.
solar-egc-690-45.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.

A design aid, not the AHJ.

baseboard-length-for-load.edition: Slant/Fin Fine Line 30 typical-curve and high-output reference (manufacturer-attributed).
baseboard-length-for-load.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed mechanical contractor govern. ACCA Manual J / D / S supersede rules of thumb.
baseboard-length-for-load.editionNote: The active length of hydronic baseboard a room's heat load needs, the inverse of baseboard-output: length = target_load / (btu_per_ft x flow_factor), with btu_per_ft the manufacturer table value interpolated at the average water temperature. Hotter water raises the output per foot and shortens the run (the main lever when a wall is too short). This is the fin-tube active length; add for the inactive ends, and the water cools along a long run so the far end puts out less (split into loops or upsize for a big load). Single-edition (manufacturer curves; quarterly recheck). The manufacturer rating at the design water temperature and the room heat loss govern.

assumptions.name: Curve table

fermentation-time-q10.formula: delta_c = (reference_temp_f - actual_temp_f) x 5 / 9; ratio = q10 ^ (delta_c / 10); predicted_time_hr = reference_time_hr x ratio.
fermentation-time-q10.edition: The Q10 temperature-coefficient rule applied to yeast fermentation, by name; a Q10 near 2.0 for baker's yeast in the working range is the value published in the standard baking-science references (Calvel, The Taste of Bread; AIB technical bulletins), cited not mirrored. The dough itself, judged by volume and the poke test, governs when it is ready.
fermentation-time-q10.freeAccess: The Q10 relation is public biology. The reference time and temperature are the bakery's own, and the Q10 value is exposed as an input rather than buried.
fermentation-time-q10.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
fermentation-time-q10.editionNote: Q10 is the factor by which a biological rate changes for a 10 degree Celsius change in temperature, and for baker's yeast across the range a bakery actually works in it is close to 2: warm the dough 10 C and it ferments twice as fast, cool it 10 C and it takes twice as long. Ten degrees Celsius is eighteen degrees Fahrenheit, which is why a ten degree Fahrenheit miss on dough temperature is worth roughly 45% on the clock, an error large enough to blow a production schedule and small enough that it routinely gets ignored. The relation scales the shop's own reference time rather than predicting one from nothing, which is what makes it usable: a bakery that knows its bulk takes two hours at a 78 F dough temperature can read today's number directly. Run the other way it answers the retarder question, since the same expression gives the ratio for any temperature the shop can hold. Across an ordinary summer-to-winter swing in an un-air-conditioned bakery the same dough can take anywhere from about 80 to about 175 minutes. A scheduling estimate; the dough, judged by volume and the poke test, governs when it is ready.

assumptions.name: Q10 near 2
assumptions.value: baker's yeast in the normal working range roughly doubles its rate per 10 C; the value is an exposed input, not a hidden constant

assumptions.name: 18 F per 10 C
assumptions.value: a 10 F miss on dough temperature is worth roughly 45% on the clock
assumptions.source: unit conversion applied to the Q10 rule

par-level-order.formula: coverage_days = lead_time_days + order_cycle_days; par_level = daily_usage x coverage_days x (1 + safety_factor); order_needed = max(0, par_level - on_hand - on_order); cases = ceil(order_needed / units_per_case); overshoot = cases x units_per_case - order_needed.
par-level-order.edition: Par level from usage across the coverage window (lead time plus order cycle) with a safety factor, the standard food-service inventory practice taught in the purchasing texts (CIA Purchasing; ServSafe management), by name; the actual usage history and the vendor's delivery reliability govern.
par-level-order.freeAccess: The par relation is arithmetic on the kitchen's own figures: usage, lead time, order cycle, safety factor, on hand, on order, and case size.
par-level-order.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
par-level-order.editionNote: A par is neither a minimum nor an average. It is the quantity that has to be on the shelf at the moment an order is placed so the kitchen does not run out before the next delivery lands, and that spans two intervals rather than one: the lead time until this order arrives, plus the full cycle until the following order arrives. Sizing a par to lead time alone is the most common way a walk-in runs dry on a Saturday, and it is the error the coverage-window line exists to prevent. The safety factor buys coverage for the days usage runs above average, and stating the trade in cases makes its cost visible: dropping the factor to zero shortens the par and the order immediately, at the price of a stockout on any above-average day. The final step is what separates the calculation from a spreadsheet, since food arrives in cases and the order is always rounded up. Reporting the raw shortfall, the whole cases, and the overshoot shows exactly how much excess the case rounding puts in the walk-in, which is where it eventually becomes waste. A purchasing estimate; the usage history and the vendor's reliability govern.

assumptions.name: Two intervals
assumptions.value: coverage = lead time + order cycle; a par sized to lead time alone runs out before the following delivery

assumptions.name: Case rounding
assumptions.value: orders round up to whole cases; the overshoot above par lands in the walk-in as excess

irrigation-uniformity.formula: Christiansen CU = 100 × (1 − Σ|x_i − mean| / (n × mean)). Distribution Uniformity DU = 100 × mean_lowest_quarter / mean_all. Pass / fail at CU 85 / DU 75.
irrigation-uniformity.edition: Christiansen 1942 paper by name; USDA NRCS National Engineering Handbook (NEH) Part 623 (Irrigation) by name.
irrigation-uniformity.freeAccess: USDA NRCS NEH Part 623 free at nrcs.usda.gov.
irrigation-uniformity.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.

acoustic-gain-pag-nag.formula: pag_db = 20log(d1_ft) + 20log(d0_ft) - 20log(ds_ft) - 20log(d2_ft) - 10log(open_mics) - 6; nag_db = 20log(d0_ft / ead_ft); the system is workable when pag_db >= nag_db.
acoustic-gain-pag-nag.edition: Potential and needed acoustic gain (PAG/NAG feedback-stability analysis; Davis & Patronis, Sound System Engineering; Yamaha Sound Reinforcement Handbook), by name; the actual room acoustics, the microphone and loudspeaker directivity, and the system tuning govern real-world stability.
acoustic-gain-pag-nag.freeAccess: The PAG/NAG relations are public sound-reinforcement engineering; the four distances, the open-mic count, and the equivalent acoustic distance are the system's layout values.
acoustic-gain-pag-nag.governance: Estimate. Head rigger and manufacturer working-load-limit charts govern. Inspect every piece of hardware before the show.
acoustic-gain-pag-nag.editionNote: A sound-reinforcement system has to be turned up loud enough for the back of the room, but every microphone also picks up the loudspeakers, and past a certain gain that loop rings into feedback. The PAG/NAG analysis checks, before feedback, whether the system can reach the level it needs. The potential acoustic gain, PAG, is how much gain the system can deliver before it becomes unstable, computed from four critical distances by the inverse-square (20 log) law: it equals 20 log of D1 plus 20 log of D0 minus 20 log of Ds minus 20 log of D2, minus 10 log of the number of open microphones, minus a 6-decibel feedback-stability margin. Here Ds is the distance from the talker to the microphone, D0 from the talker to the farthest listener, D1 from the loudspeaker to the farthest listener, and D2 from the loudspeaker to the microphone; each doubling of the number of open microphones (NOM) costs 3 decibels, and the 6-decibel margin keeps the system a safe distance below the ring point. The needed acoustic gain, NAG, is how much the system must amplify so the farthest listener hears as well as they would standing at a comfortable close distance to the unaided talker: it is 20 log of D0 divided by the equivalent acoustic distance, EAD, the reference close distance. The system is workable when PAG is at least NAG. For a talker-to-mic distance of 2 feet, a talker-to-farthest-listener distance of 30 feet, a loudspeaker-to-farthest-listener distance of 8 feet, a loudspeaker-to-mic distance of 12 feet, one open microphone, and a 6-foot equivalent acoustic distance, PAG works out to 14.0 decibels and NAG to 14.0 decibels, exactly balanced -- the textbook marginal case. Moving the microphone in to 1 foot from the talker raises PAG to about 20 decibels, giving 6 decibels of comfortable headroom. The design levers follow directly: put the microphone close to the talker, which has the largest effect; put the loudspeaker close to the listeners and away from the microphone; and keep the number of open microphones to a minimum. This is a design screen; the real room acoustics, the directivity of the microphones and loudspeakers, and the final system tuning govern actual stability.

assumptions.name: PAG/NAG
assumptions.value: PAG = 20log(D1)+20log(D0)-20log(Ds)-20log(D2)-10log(NOM)-6; NAG = 20log(D0/EAD); workable when PAG >= NAG

assumptions.name: Design levers
assumptions.value: mic close to the talker (biggest effect), speaker close to listeners and away from the mic, minimize open mics (each doubling = -3 dB); 6 dB feedback margin

chain-hoist-lift-time.formula: lift_time_min = lift_height_ft / hoist_speed_fpm; hoisting_hp = load_lb x hoist_speed_fpm / 33000; allowed_on_time_min = duty_cycle x rating_period_min; lifts_per_period = allowed_on_time_min / lift_time_min.
chain-hoist-lift-time.edition: Lift time from height and rated speed, hoisting horsepower from load x speed / 33,000, and intermittent-duty on-time from the motor's rated duty cycle over its rating period, by name; duty ratings and load charts are the hoist manufacturer's, and ANSI E1.6 entertainment hoist standards and the venue's qualified rigger govern. The distro is sized on inrush, not on this steady figure.
chain-hoist-lift-time.freeAccess: The relations are public mechanics (33,000 ft-lb per minute per horsepower). The hoist speed, duty cycle, and rating period are read off the equipment the user has.
chain-hoist-lift-time.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
chain-hoist-lift-time.editionNote: The first line is the schedule, and it is the one nobody estimates correctly by eye, because hoist speed varies by an order of magnitude across the hoists on a single truck: sixteen feet per minute for a standard motor, thirty-two or sixty-four for a high-speed one. A hundred lifts at four minutes each is most of a day. The duty-cycle lines are the ones that surprise people. An electric chain hoist is rated for intermittent duty, and a common rating allows the motor to run forty percent of a ten-minute period -- four minutes on, six minutes off. Run it harder and the motor overheats, and that failure is not graceful. On a long trim a single full-height lift can consume most of the allowed on-time by itself, which is why a rig that has to come in and out repeatedly during a show is planned around duty cycle rather than around hoist count, and why the answer to a tight cue is a faster hoist or a shorter trim rather than a longer press of the button. Note that the hoisting horsepower comes out under one for a typical one-ton hoist: chain hoist motors are small, and the number that sizes the distribution is the inrush current at start, not this steady figure.

assumptions.name: Horsepower
assumptions.value: 33,000 ft-lb per minute per horsepower; hoisting hp = load x speed / 33,000

assumptions.name: Intermittent duty
assumptions.value: a common entertainment hoist rating is 40% over a 10-minute period; exceeding it overheats the motor

assumptions.name: Distro sizing
assumptions.value: the feeder is sized on motor INRUSH, not on the steady hoisting horsepower

dti.edition: FNMA Single-Family Selling Guide §B3-6-02 (current). FHA Handbook 4000.1 §II.A.5. VA Lenders Handbook M26-7.
dti.freeAccess: Free at selling-guide.fanniemae.com, hud.gov, and benefits.va.gov.

statistics-quickread.formula: Standard descriptive statistics. mean = sum / n; sample variance = sum((x_i - mean)^2) / (n-1); population variance = sum((x_i - mean)^2) / n; standard deviation = sqrt(variance).
statistics-quickread.edition: Classical descriptive statistics; physical / mathematical fact. The sample-vs-population distinction is the Bessel-correction convention (Bessel 1838).
statistics-quickread.freeAccess: No code citation required. Any introductory statistics text covers these.
statistics-quickread.governance: Estimate only. Readability formulas and similar metrics are derived from a representative population and have known edge-case noise. The classroom teacher governs final text selection, grade placement, and assessment decisions.
statistics-quickread.editionNote: Single-edition (mathematical fact). The sample-variance formula uses n-1; the population-variance formula uses n. Pick the one your assignment specifies.

lighting-uniformity-ratio.formula: avg/min, max/min, U0 = min/avg over a grid of readings; pass if avg/min <= target and max/min <= target.
lighting-uniformity-ratio.edition: The IES illuminance uniformity ratios (avg/min, max/min, U0), by name.
lighting-uniformity-ratio.freeAccess: The uniformity ratios and target values are published in the IES recommended practices for each space type. The IES RP governs the target.
lighting-uniformity-ratio.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
lighting-uniformity-ratio.editionNote: Illuminance uniformity from a grid of readings: average-to-minimum (avg/min), maximum-to-minimum (max/min), and the minimum-to-average uniformity U0 = min/avg. Common targets run about 3:1 max/min for offices and tighter for tasks. The same rough average can hide a patchy layout - a bright-under, dark-between-fixtures pattern that only the ratio reveals. This returns the ratios and an optional pass/fail against the entered targets: it treats the readings as an equal-weight grid and does not verify the measurement grid spacing or the meter calibration. A design aid; the IES recommended practice for the space type governs the target.

crown-pruning-dose.formula: removal_pct = removed_foliage / live_foliage x 100; cap_pct = mature 25 / young 15 / over-mature 10 / stressed 0; within when removal_pct <= cap_pct.
crown-pruning-dose.edition: ANSI A300 Part 1 5.5.3 (not more than 25% of the foliage in an annual growing season, adjusted for species, age, health and site) and ISA Best Management Practices - Pruning, by name.
crown-pruning-dose.freeAccess: The A300 removal-limit percentages are published arboricultural practice; a qualified arborist governs the actual dose.
crown-pruning-dose.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
crown-pruning-dose.editionNote: The 25% ceiling (A300 Part 1 5.5.3) is a maximum for one growing season, not a target. A300 says to adjust it for species, age, health and site but gives no other numbers; the young (15%), over-mature (10%) and stressed (0%) caps are this tile's conservative adjustments - a stressed tree should not have live foliage removed until it recovers; lion's-tailing (stripping interior foliage, leaving tufts at the branch ends) violates A300 even when the total removed is under the percent cap; removing too much live foliage starves the tree. A planning aid, not an arborist's prescription.

assumptions.name: Class caps
assumptions.value: mature <= 25% single season (A300); young 15%, over-mature 10%, stressed 0% are conservative planning adjustments

assumptions.name: Lion's-tailing
assumptions.value: stripping interior foliage violates A300 even under the percent cap

projectile-range.formula: t = (v sin(theta) + sqrt((v sin(theta))^2 + 2 g h))/g; R = v cos(theta) t; H = v^2 sin^2(theta)/(2g) above the launch; best angle = atan(v/sqrt(v^2 + 2 g h)); g = 32.174 ft/s^2. On level ground (h = 0) R = v^2 sin(2 theta)/g, peaking at 45 deg with complementary angles giving equal range.
projectile-range.edition: The level-ground projectile relations R = v^2 sin(2 theta)/g, H = v^2 sin^2(theta)/(2g), t = 2 v sin(theta)/g (standard kinematics), by name.
projectile-range.freeAccess: The projectile relations are standard published kinematics; the launch speed and angle are the user's inputs.
projectile-range.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
projectile-range.editionNote: Still-air, level-ground trajectory of a point projectile launched at speed v and angle theta above horizontal: horizontal range R = v^2 sin(2 theta)/g, maximum height H = v^2 sin^2(theta)/(2g), and time of flight t = 2 v sin(theta)/g, with g = 32.174 ft/s^2. The range peaks at 45 degrees; any two complementary angles (for example 30 and 60 degrees) give the SAME range but different heights and hang times, the trade a nozzle operator or a sprinkler layout makes between reach, height, and coverage. Air resistance is NEGLECTED, so a real water stream or light object falls short of these numbers - they are the still-air upper bound. A launch height above the landing plane is an input: the flight time becomes (v sin(theta) + sqrt((v sin(theta))^2 + 2 g h))/g and the longest reach moves below 45 degrees, to atan(v/sqrt(v^2 + 2 g h)); wind and stream break-up are separate. Use it for reach and clearance estimates, not a ballistic or aerodynamic calculation. A planning estimate; field conditions govern.

assumptions.name: Range/height/time
assumptions.value: R = v^2 sin(2 theta)/g, H = v^2 sin^2(theta)/(2g), t = 2 v sin(theta)/g

assumptions.name: Optimal angle
assumptions.value: range peaks at 45 deg; complementary angles give equal range

assumptions.name: No drag
assumptions.value: still-air upper bound; air resistance shortens a real stream, launch height/wind are separate

partition-mass-law-tl.formula: TL = 20 log10(m f) - 47 dB (field/random incidence), or - 42 (normal incidence); m the surface mass in kg/m^2 (lb/ft^2 x 4.88243), f in Hz. +6 dB per doubling of m or f.
partition-mass-law-tl.edition: First-principles panel acoustics - the limp-mass law - as given in Bies & Hansen, Engineering Noise Control, and FHWA highway-noise guidance, by name.
partition-mass-law-tl.freeAccess: The mass law TL = 20 log10(m f) - 47 is standard published acoustics (Bies & Hansen; FHWA public highway-noise material); the surface mass and frequency are the user's inputs.
partition-mass-law-tl.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
partition-mass-law-tl.editionNote: The single-panel mass-law transmission loss, the partition-attenuation member the room-acoustics family (reverberation, levels, absorption) leaves out. A limp, non-rigid panel resists airborne sound in proportion to its surface mass and the frequency: TL = 20 log10(m f) - 47 dB for random (field) incidence, or - 42 for normal incidence, with m in kg/m^2 (entered in lb/ft^2 and converted at 1 lb/ft^2 = 4.88243 kg/m^2) and f in Hz. The signature is +6 dB per doubling of either mass or frequency. A single 1/2 in gypsum layer (~2 lb/ft^2) gives about 27 dB at 500 Hz. This is the IDEALIZED mass law only: it does not capture the coincidence (critical-frequency) dip where TL falls sharply, the stiffness-controlled low-frequency region, cavity or stud resonances, flanking paths, or leaks, and it is NOT the ASTM E413 Sound Transmission Class (STC), a single-number rating fit to the whole third-octave TL spectrum. Use it to compare bare single-leaf partitions and to see the mass and frequency trends; a lab-tested assembly rating and the acoustician govern.

assumptions.name: Mass law
assumptions.value: TL = 20 log10(m f) - 47 (field) or - 42 (normal); +6 dB per doubling of m or f

assumptions.name: Idealized single leaf
assumptions.value: excludes the coincidence dip, stiffness region, cavity/stud resonances, flanking, and leaks

assumptions.name: Not STC
assumptions.value: the closed-form mass-law TL, not the ASTM E413 STC single-number rating

guide-rail-bracket-span.formula: moment = P x span / 4 for a concentrated load at midspan; stress = moment / section modulus; deflection = P x span cubed / (48 E I); maximum span for a deflection limit = the cube root of (limit x 48 E I / P).
guide-rail-bracket-span.edition: Simple-span beam relations for a concentrated load at midspan, by name, with ASME A17.1 named as governing the load cases, allowable stresses and deflections, rail sections, and bracket and fastening requirements that determine acceptability.
guide-rail-bracket-span.freeAccess: Textbook beam formulas on rail section properties and loads the user supplies; no rail table or code allowable is reproduced.
guide-rail-bracket-span.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
guide-rail-bracket-span.editionNote: A guide rail spans between brackets like any beam, carrying the horizontal load at the guide shoes as a concentrated load. For a concentrated load at midspan the moment goes as the span and the deflection as its cube, so halving the span halves the moment and cuts the deflection to an eighth. A rail that is marginal on deflection is therefore usually fixed by adding a bracket rather than by upsizing the rail, which matters because rails are a long-lead item and brackets are not: matching an eighth of the deflection by section alone would take eight times the moment of inertia, several sizes of rail. The governing load is safety application, not normal operation. When the car safeties set, they clamp the rails and transmit a large force, and the rail and its brackets have to take it without permanent deformation; normal eccentric loading, a heavy load in one corner of the car, is a much smaller number that governs the deflection limit rather than the strength. Seismic is the case that changes everything in higher-hazard regions: the code's provisions require larger rail sections, closer brackets, retainer plates, and additional devices, and a rail arrangement designed for a low-seismic building is not adequate when the same design is used elsewhere, which is a common source of trouble on repeat-design buildings.

assumptions.name: Add a bracket, do not upsize the rail
assumptions.value: deflection goes as the cube of the span for a midspan point load, so halving it buys an eighth

assumptions.name: Safety application governs strength
assumptions.value: eccentric car loading is much smaller and governs the deflection limit instead

assumptions.name: The bracket and its fastening are the frequent weak element
assumptions.value: and neither is evaluated by a rail beam calculation

blast-burden-spacing.formula: burden = burden ratio x hole diameter / 12; spacing = spacing ratio x burden; subdrill and stemming are their own ratios of the burden; stiffness ratio = bench height / burden, and the largest hole a bench supports = bench height x 12 / (2 x burden ratio).
blast-burden-spacing.edition: The published pattern ratios by name -- burden ratio typically 20 to 35, spacing 1.15 to 1.4 times the burden staggered, subdrill 0.2 to 0.5, stemming 0.7 to 1.0 x burden and never under 20 hole diameters -- with the stiffness check requiring bench height at least twice the burden. Starting-point geometry only. Blasting is a licensed activity: the blaster in charge, the state and federal explosives regulations, MSHA or OSHA jurisdiction, and the site's blast plan govern.
blast-burden-spacing.freeAccess: Ratio arithmetic on published starting ranges the user enters; no proprietary design data is reproduced.
blast-burden-spacing.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
blast-burden-spacing.editionNote: Every dimension in a blast pattern is a multiple of either the hole diameter or the burden, which is why one ratio propagates through the whole design. The burden ratio carries the rock and the explosive together: a low ratio near 20 suits hard rock or a low-energy product, a high one near 35 suits soft rock and a high-energy product. Stiffness ratio is the check that stops a bad pattern before it is drilled. A bench whose height is less than about twice the burden cannot break properly to the free face -- the charge behaves like a crater instead, venting upward, and the result is airblast, flyrock, and poor fragmentation. On a shallow bench the answer is a smaller diameter and a tighter pattern, not the same holes spread further apart, and this ratio is what makes that argument quantitatively rather than by assertion. These are a first design to be adjusted against the rock actually in the face: jointing, bedding, mud seams, voids, and a variable free face all move the correct burden more than the ratios do, and a burden right on one end of a bench can be wrong on the other. The ratios assume a vertical or near-vertical hole to a clean free face with adequate relief.

assumptions.name: One ratio sets the whole pattern
assumptions.value: every dimension is a multiple of the diameter or the burden

assumptions.name: Stiffness below 2 is a crater, not a bench
assumptions.value: and the fix is a smaller hole, never a wider pattern

assumptions.name: The face governs, not the ratios
assumptions.value: jointing, mud seams, and a variable free face move the correct burden more

gas-fuel-conversion.formula: cfh = appliance input / heating value for each fuel; orifice flow Q ~ area x sqrt(pressure / specific gravity), so holding input the area ratio = (cfh_to / cfh_from) x sqrt((p_from / sg_from) / (p_to / sg_to)).
gas-fuel-conversion.edition: First-principles orifice flow holding appliance input (public); the NG/LP heating values, specific gravities, and manifold pressures are editable defaults.
gas-fuel-conversion.freeAccess: The orifice-flow relation is public physics; the manufacturer's listed conversion kit governs.
gas-fuel-conversion.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
gas-fuel-conversion.editionNote: Single-edition (the equipment manufacturer's listed NG/LP conversion kit and the AHJ govern).

assumptions.name: Defaults
assumptions.value: NG/LP heating values 1030 / 2500 BTU/cf, specific gravities 0.60 / 1.52, manifold pressures 3.5 / 11.0 in. w.c., all editable

assumptions.name: Orifice model
assumptions.value: flow goes as area x sqrt(pressure / specific gravity); the area ratio holds appliance input across the fuel change

assumptions.name: Field drilling
assumptions.value: field orifice drilling is generally prohibited; install the listed manufacturer conversion kit

door-maneuvering-clearance.formula: pull side: required depth 60 in perpendicular to the doorway AND 18 in clear beyond the latch side; push side with no closer and no latch: required depth 48 in and no latch-side strip. Footprint = required depth x (door clear width + required latch-side clearance).
door-maneuvering-clearance.edition: 2010 ADA Standards for Accessible Design 404.2.4.1, front approach at manual swinging doors and gates - maneuvering space on the pull side extending 18 in minimum beyond the latch side and 60 in minimum perpendicular to the doorway, and on the push side of doors not equipped with a closer or latch, space the same width as the door opening extending 48 in minimum perpendicular to the doorway.
door-maneuvering-clearance.freeAccess: The 2010 ADA Standards are a US federal regulation published in full at no cost by the Access Board and the Department of Justice. Only the front-approach rows are used; the rest of Table 404.2.4.1 is not reproduced.
door-maneuvering-clearance.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
door-maneuvering-clearance.editionNote: The asymmetry is the point, and putting a number on it is what the tile adds. A 32 in door needs a 60 by 50 in footprint on the pull side - 20.8 sq ft - and only 48 by 32 on the push side, 10.7 sq ft. Nearly a factor of two for the same door, which means a layout that clears on the push side tells you nothing at all about the pull side, and both faces have to work. The latch-side strip is the specific thing people forget, because it is empty WALL rather than door and does not read as part of the opening on a plan: it is exactly where a corner, a corridor wall, a vanity, or a light switch kills an otherwise legal door, and the common 12 in that gets left is 6 in short of the 18 required. SCOPE, and it matters: only the FRONT approach is reproduced. Table 404.2.4.1 also covers hinge-side and latch-side approaches, which have different and generally larger requirements, and it ADDS clearance where a door has both a closer and a latch - including on the push side, where none is otherwise required. A door with a closer is the ordinary commercial case, so the push-side numbers here do not apply to it, and the note says to read the table rather than pretending this covers it. Also not checked: the 32 in clear width at 90 degrees, the level and unobstructed condition of the clearance floor and its 1:48 maximum slope, opening force and closing speed, threshold height, hardware type and mounting height, doors in series, and the accessible route leading to the door. The 2010 ADA Standards and ANSI A117.1 differ in places and a state may adopt either, which is why the minimums are editable inputs. A screen, not a certification of accessibility; the adopted standard and the AHJ govern.

assumptions.name: Pull side, front approach
assumptions.value: 60 in perpendicular and 18 in beyond the latch side

assumptions.name: Push side, front approach
assumptions.value: 48 in perpendicular, door width only, for a door with NO closer and NO latch

assumptions.name: Asymmetry
assumptions.value: the pull side demands roughly twice the footprint; both faces must work

assumptions.name: Front approach only
assumptions.value: hinge-side and latch-side rows, and the closer-plus-latch additions, are not reproduced

assumptions.name: Not checked
assumptions.value: clear width, floor slope, opening force, threshold, hardware, doors in series, the route

sprinkler-gpm-for-precip.formula: required_gpm = target_precip_in_hr x zone_ft2 / 96.3, the inverse of precip_in_hr = 96.3 x zone_gpm / zone_ft2 (the 96.3 constant = 231 in^3/gal / 144 in^2/ft^2 x 60 min/hr spreads 1 gpm over 1 ft^2).
sprinkler-gpm-for-precip.edition: First-principles precipitation-rate relation with the Irrigation Association design references and the Rain Bird / Hunter design manuals (by name), solved for the flow; no edition cycle.
sprinkler-gpm-for-precip.freeAccess: The precipitation-rate relation and the 96.3 constant are public irrigation-design practice. The nozzle chart and the matched-precipitation rule are in the manufacturer's design manuals.
sprinkler-gpm-for-precip.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
sprinkler-gpm-for-precip.editionNote: Single-edition (the 96.3 conversion and the matched-precipitation rule do not roll), solved for the zone flow: the total head flow a target precipitation rate needs over the covered area, so the designer picks nozzles from the manufacturer's chart at the operating pressure that sum to about this gpm. This is a design-rate estimate, not a system audit (irrigation-uniformity audits the installed result).

assumptions.name: Precipitation-rate relation
assumptions.value: required gpm = target PR (in/hr) x zone area (ft^2) / 96.3

assumptions.name: Head flows
assumptions.value: the per-head flows are the manufacturer's nozzle-chart values at the operating pressure

assumptions.name: Matched precipitation
assumptions.value: sprays (~1.5-2 in/hr) and rotors (~0.4-0.8 in/hr) apply water at very different rates and must not share a valve

ashrae-622-ventilation.formula: q_tot = 0.03 x floor_area_ft2 + 7.5 x (bedrooms + 1); q_fan = max(0, q_tot - Phi x infil_credit_cfm x Aext), Phi = 1 balanced or infil_credit / q_tot unbalanced (ASHRAE 62.2 Eq. 4.2); verdict = q_fan > 0 (fan required) else (credit meets Qtot).
ashrae-622-ventilation.edition: ASHRAE 62.2-2019 §4.1 whole-house ventilation rate (Qtot = 0.03 x Afloor + 7.5 x (Nbr + 1)) and the fan flow Qfan = Qtot - Phi (Qinf x Aext) (Eq. 4.2), by name; the 0.03 cfm/ft^2 and 7.5 cfm/person are the standard's rate coefficients.
ashrae-622-ventilation.freeAccess: The whole-house ventilation rate and the fan-flow relation are stated in ASHRAE 62.2-2019 §4.1; the arithmetic is public. The infiltration credit comes from the measured air-tightness.
ashrae-622-ventilation.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
ashrae-622-ventilation.editionNote: ASHRAE 62.2-2019 §4.1 gives Qtot = 0.03 x Afloor + 7.5 x (Nbr + 1) and the fan flow Qfan = Qtot - Phi (Qinf x Aext) (Eq. 4.2), where Qinf is the infiltration credit, Phi = 1 for a balanced system and Qinf / Qtot for an exhaust- or supply-only one, and Aext = 1 for a detached house or the exterior share of the envelope for an attached unit. The bedroom count is the standard's occupancy proxy (occupants assumed = Nbr + 1); the infiltration credit comes from the measured air-tightness per the 62.2 infiltration method (the conservative default is zero credit, sizing the fan to the full Qtot); local exhaust (kitchen and bath) is a separate 62.2 requirement this tile does not cover. A sizing aid, not a 62.2 compliance certificate.

assumptions.name: Total required Qtot
assumptions.value: Qtot = 0.03 x conditioned floor area + 7.5 x (bedrooms + 1); occupants assumed Nbr + 1

assumptions.name: Fan flow
assumptions.value: Qfan = max(0, Qtot - Phi x infiltration credit x Aext), Phi = 1 balanced or Qinf / Qtot unbalanced; the tighter the house, the smaller the credit and the larger the fan

assumptions.name: Infiltration credit
assumptions.value: the credit is the blower-door natural infiltration; the conservative default is zero

pv-array-sizing.formula: specific_yield = psh x 365 x perf_ratio; dc_kw = target_annual_kwh / specific_yield; monthly_kwh_avg = target_annual_kwh / 12.
pv-array-sizing.edition: NREL PVWatts energy model (E_annual = P_dc x PSH x 365 x PR) solved for the array size, the inverse of the PV energy-yield tile, by name; the relations are public.
pv-array-sizing.freeAccess: The PVWatts energy model is a public NREL relation; PVWatts is free at pvwatts.nrel.gov.
pv-array-sizing.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
pv-array-sizing.editionNote: The NREL PVWatts energy model inverted for the array size: P_dc = E_target / (PSH x 365 x PR). The specific yield PSH x 365 x PR (kWh per kWp) is the site's annual production per installed kW, so the required DC nameplate is the target annual energy divided by it. The peak-sun-hours is the plane-of-array daily irradiation from NREL's NSRDB / PVWatts for the site, tilt, and azimuth (not a fixed 5); the performance ratio (default 0.77, a typical whole-system ratio including temperature loss; it equals the retired PVWatts V1 derate -- current PVWatts uses 14% losses and a 96% inverter, 0.826) is the single biggest lever, and the array must be oversized slightly to cover degradation over its life. A pre-design estimate, not a bankable production model; module count and roof area then follow.

assumptions.name: Array size
assumptions.value: dc_kw = target_annual_kwh / (psh x 365 x perf_ratio) (PVWatts inverted)

assumptions.name: Performance ratio
assumptions.value: PR (default 0.77) rolls up soiling, shading, mismatch, wiring, inverter, and availability losses

assumptions.name: Specific yield
assumptions.value: psh x 365 x PR is the site's kWh per installed kWp

motor-overload-sizing.formula: hi_class = (sf >= 1.15) or (marked rise <= 40 degC); mult = hi_class ? 1.25 : 1.15; mult_max = hi_class ? 1.40 : 1.30; ol_A = fla_A x mult; ol_max_A = fla_A x mult_max.
motor-overload-sizing.edition: Motor running-overload sizing on the nameplate full-load current under NEC 2023 430.32(A)(1) (125% for a marked service factor of 1.15 or more or a marked temperature rise of 40 degC or less, 115% otherwise) with the 430.32(C) will-not-start ceiling (140%/130%), by name. A computational aid; the AHJ-adopted NEC edition governs.
motor-overload-sizing.freeAccess: NEC is free to read at nfpa.org/freeaccess. The 430.32(D) hand-started small motor and 430.36 fuse-as-overload are stated as out of scope, not modeled; a thermal protector integral with the motor is the 430.32(A)(2) option (added 2026-10-08), and a motor of 1 hp or less, automatically started, is the 430.32(B) option (added 2026-10-09).
motor-overload-sizing.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed electrician govern. Verify against the NEC edition adopted in your jurisdiction.
motor-overload-sizing.editionNote: Editions available: bundled values follow NEC 2023. NEC 2026 is the current published edition; jurisdictions on NEC 2017 / 2020 / 2023 / 2026 use slightly different ambient corrections and ampacity ranges; verify the edition adopted by your AHJ.

assumptions.name: Basis current
assumptions.value: the motor NAMEPLATE FLA, not the 430.6 table FLC the 430.52 branch device uses

assumptions.name: Class selection
assumptions.value: 125%/140% for marked SF >= 1.15 or marked rise <= 40 degC; 115%/130% otherwise; an unmarked (blank) value does not qualify

assumptions.name: Scope
assumptions.value: a continuous-duty motor over 1 hp, or 1 hp or less automatically started, with a separate overload device or an integral thermal protector

assumptions.name: Thermal protector option
assumptions.value: ultimate trip no more than 170% (9 A or less), 156% (9.1-20 A), or 140% (over 20 A) of the TABLE full-load current

assumptions.name: 1 hp or less, automatically started
assumptions.value: a separate device takes the same 125%/115% rule and 430.32(C) ceiling; an integral thermal protector has no percentage ceiling, only approval for the motor it protects

boring-bar-max-overhang.formula: I = pi d^4/64; L_max = (3 E I delta_allow / F)^(1/3); L/d ratio for chatter risk. (E = 30e6 psi steel, ~90e6 carbide)
boring-bar-max-overhang.edition: The cantilever tip-deflection model delta = F L^3/(3 E I) with I = pi d^4/64 solved for the overhang, a standard mechanics-of-materials result applied to tool overhang, by name.
boring-bar-max-overhang.freeAccess: The cantilever deflection formula is a public mechanics-of-materials result; the L/d overhang limits are standard machining guidance.
boring-bar-max-overhang.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
boring-bar-max-overhang.editionNote: The longest overhang before the tip deflection reaches the allowable, the inverse of boring-bar-deflection: from delta = F L^3/(3 E I), L_max = (3 E I delta / F)^(1/3), with I = pi d^4/64 and E = 30e6 psi steel / ~90e6 carbide. Deflection is only half the story: the reported L/d must be checked against the chatter limit (~4:1 steel, ~6:1 to 8:1 carbide); if the deflection-limited overhang exceeds the chatter L/d, chatter governs and the real max overhang is the shorter one. Because deflection scales with L^3, this length is a hard wall. A uniform solid round cantilever under a tip point load (a stepped or hollow bar changes I; a real cut adds a dynamic/regenerative-chatter component this static estimate does not capture). A shop aid; the tool and setup govern.

assumptions.name: Cantilever inverse
assumptions.value: L_max = (3 E I delta / F)^(1/3), I = pi d^4/64, uniform solid round bar under a tip load

assumptions.name: Chatter may govern
assumptions.value: check the L/d against ~4:1 steel / 6-8:1 carbide; if exceeded, the chatter limit sets a shorter max overhang

assumptions.name: Static estimate
assumptions.value: static solid-round model, not a stability-lobe analysis

reynolds-number-pipe.formula: Re = V (D/12) / nu; regime = Re < 2,300 laminar, <= 4,000 transitional, else turbulent.
reynolds-number-pipe.edition: The Reynolds number Re = V D / nu (= rho V D / mu) and the standard pipe-flow transition bands, with a 60 degF water kinematic viscosity of about 1.21e-5 ft^2/s, a standard fluid-mechanics result, by name.
reynolds-number-pipe.freeAccess: The Reynolds-number definition and the pipe-flow transition bands are public results in any fluid-mechanics reference.
reynolds-number-pipe.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
reynolds-number-pipe.editionNote: The Reynolds number Re = V D / nu (= rho V D / mu), the pipe-flow transition bands (laminar below ~2,300, turbulent above ~4,000, transitional between), and a 60 degF water kinematic viscosity of about 1.21e-5 ft^2/s (1.13 centistokes). This returns the Reynolds number and regime for full pipe flow - it uses the entered kinematic viscosity (temperature- and fluid-dependent; provide the value for the fluid and temperature at hand), assumes a circular full pipe, and does not itself compute the friction factor or head loss. An engineering aid; the fluid property data at the operating condition govern.

assumptions.name: Reynolds number
assumptions.value: Re = V D / nu, velocity times diameter over kinematic viscosity

assumptions.name: Regime bands
assumptions.value: laminar below ~2,300, transitional ~2,300 to 4,000, turbulent above ~4,000

assumptions.name: Viscosity
assumptions.value: entered per fluid and temperature; ~1.21e-5 ft^2/s for 60 degF water

channel-froude-number.formula: V = Q/(b y); Fr = V/sqrt(g y) (g = 32.2, D = y rectangular); regime by Fr vs 1; q = Q/b; yc = (q^2/g)^(1/3).
channel-froude-number.edition: The open-channel Froude-number regime classification Fr = V/sqrt(g D) and the rectangular critical depth yc = (q^2/g)^(1/3), as compiled in Chow's Open-Channel Hydraulics, by name.
channel-froude-number.freeAccess: The Froude-number classification and the rectangular critical-depth relation are public results in the standard open-channel-hydraulics references.
channel-froude-number.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
channel-froude-number.editionNote: The Froude number Fr = V/sqrt(g D) (g = 32.2 ft/s^2, D = A/T the hydraulic depth, equal to y for a wide/rectangular section), the subcritical/critical/supercritical regimes at Fr <> 1, and the rectangular critical depth yc = (q^2/g)^(1/3) with q = Q/b, as compiled in Chow's open-channel-hydraulics reference. This returns the regime and rectangular critical depth for a prismatic rectangular channel - it uses D = y (rectangular), does not compute the normal depth (that is Manning), the hydraulic-jump conjugate depth, or a trapezoidal/irregular section's critical depth. A design aid, not a substitute for a licensed engineer's hydraulic design; the engineer of record governs.

assumptions.name: Froude number
assumptions.value: Fr = V/sqrt(g y) for a rectangular section; Fr < 1 subcritical, > 1 supercritical

assumptions.name: Critical depth
assumptions.value: yc = (q^2/g)^(1/3) with q = Q/b; flow is subcritical when y > yc

assumptions.name: Scope
assumptions.value: prismatic rectangular channel; normal depth (Manning) and the hydraulic jump are separate

concrete-anchor-pullout.formula: Np = 8 x head_bearing_area_in2 x fc_psi; Npn = psi_cP x Np (psi_cP = 1.4 uncracked at service, 1.0 cracked); phiNpn = 0.70 x Npn.
concrete-anchor-pullout.edition: The ACI 318-19 Section 17.6.3 headed-anchor pullout in tension, by name.
concrete-anchor-pullout.freeAccess: ACI 318 is available through ACI; the 17.6.3 pullout provisions are published design equations.
concrete-anchor-pullout.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
concrete-anchor-pullout.editionNote: Pullout does not depend on embedment - deepening the anchor does not raise it (that is the breakout mode). It applies to headed anchors where the head bears on the concrete, not to adhesive or expansion anchors (which use a tested bond or slip value). Abrg is the net bearing area of the head or nut. The 1.4 uncracked factor applies only when analysis shows the concrete stays uncracked at service load; use 1.0 otherwise. phi = 0.70 is Condition B (no supplementary reinforcement). ACI 318 Chapter 17 and the engineer of record govern - a design check, not a stamped anchor design.

assumptions.name: Embedment-independent
assumptions.value: pullout Np = 8 Abrg f'c depends on the head area, not the embedment depth

assumptions.name: Uncracked bonus
assumptions.value: psi_cP = 1.4 only when analysis shows the concrete stays uncracked at service; else 1.0

corner-bead-takeoff.formula: corner_lf = corners x height; wrap_lf = openings x (2 x height + width); total = (corner_lf + wrap_lf) x (1 + waste); sticks = max(ceil(total/stock), one-stick-per-run count).
corner-bead-takeoff.edition: Straight takeoff arithmetic with one trade rule encoded - bead is not spliced mid-run - so the stick count takes the larger of the LF division and the per-run floor. No standard claimed.
corner-bead-takeoff.freeAccess: Counting arithmetic; the no-splice practice is universal finishing guidance published freely by bead manufacturers.
corner-bead-takeoff.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
corner-bead-takeoff.editionNote: The per-run floor is the part a pure LF calculator gets wrong: 9 corners of 8 ft on 10-ft stock divide to 12 sticks but need 15, because each corner is one unspliced stick and each wrapped opening is three. Metal, vinyl, and paper-faced bead count the same way; archway and bullnose profiles count per the manufacturer. Mud and tape quantities are the separate drywall tile; wood casing is trim-linear-footage. The finish schedule and the crew's stock preference govern.

assumptions.name: No mid-run splices
assumptions.value: each corner leg and each wrap leg/head is at least one full stick
assumptions.source: universal finishing practice (a splice telegraphs through the mud)

assumptions.name: Wrap geometry
assumptions.value: a cased opening wrapped in bead takes two legs plus a head

concrete-maturity.formula: M = (Ta - T0) x hours in deg C-hr (Nurse-Saul, one constant-temperature interval); te = exp(-Q x (1/(Ta+273.15) - 1/(Tr+273.15))) x hours (Arrhenius equivalent age, kelvin); target_hours = target_TTF / (Ta - T0) when a calibrated target is given.
concrete-maturity.edition: ASTM C1074 (Standard Practice for Estimating Concrete Strength by the Maturity Method), by name; both maturity functions with their recommended Type I no-admixture constants.
concrete-maturity.freeAccess: The Nurse-Saul and Arrhenius maturity functions and the recommended constants are stated in ASTM C1074 and reproduced across the public maturity literature (NRMCA CIP 39); the arithmetic is public.
concrete-maturity.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
concrete-maturity.editionNote: ASTM C1074 maturity method: the Nurse-Saul time-temperature factor M = Sum (Ta - T0) x dt in deg C-hr, evaluated over one constant-temperature interval, with the recommended datum T0 = 0 C (32 F) for Type I cement without admixtures cured 0 to 40 C (otherwise per the C1074 datum procedure); and the Arrhenius equivalent age te = exp(-Q x (1/Ta - 1/Tr)) x t with temperatures in kelvin, Q = 5000 K for Type I without admixtures, and the traditional reference Tr = 20 C (68 F; C1074 permits others such as 23 C; both ship editable). Intervals at or below the datum accrue no maturity. The strength a TTF represents comes only from the lab-developed strength-maturity relationship for the project's own materials and mix (the C1074 calibration procedure); the field TTF is compared to that calibrated target. A scheduling estimate that supplements, not replaces, acceptance cylinders; the engineer of record and the project specification govern.

assumptions.name: Datum and Q
assumptions.value: T0 = 0 C and Q = 5000 K are the C1074 recommendations for Type I cement without admixtures; other mixes calibrate their own

assumptions.name: Single interval
assumptions.value: one average temperature over the period; a logged history sums interval by interval

assumptions.name: Calibration governs
assumptions.value: TTF maps to strength only through the lab curve for the actual mix; acceptance cylinders are not replaced

brick-veneer-anchor-spacing.formula: anchors = ceil(area / area_per_anchor); area_per = 2.67 ft^2 typical (2.0 high-demand); max 32 in horizontal, 25 in vertical spacing (TMS 402; the IRC R703.8.4 cap is 24 in).
brick-veneer-anchor-spacing.edition: TMS 402 (Building Code Requirements for Masonry Structures) and IBC 1405 veneer-anchor provisions, by name.
brick-veneer-anchor-spacing.freeAccess: The veneer-anchor area and spacing limits are in TMS 402 and IBC Chapter 14 (many jurisdictions post the adopted IBC). TMS 402 / IBC and the engineer of record govern.
brick-veneer-anchor-spacing.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
brick-veneer-anchor-spacing.editionNote: Brick-veneer anchor count per TMS 402 / IBC 1405: one anchor per no more than the entered wall area (2.67 ft^2 typical, 2.0 ft^2 for high wind/seismic demand), with maximum spacing of 32 in horizontal and 25 in vertical (TMS 402 / BIA Technical Note 28; the IRC caps vertical spacing at 24 in). The count = ceil(area / area-per-anchor); a tighter demand limit adds anchors on a denser grid, and if the max horizontal x vertical grid is smaller than the area limit, the spacing caps govern. This returns the count and grid for the entered limits: the area-per-anchor and spacing caps depend on the adopted edition, the anchor type, and the wind/seismic demand, and it does not design the anchor itself. A detailing aid; TMS 402 / IBC and the engineer of record govern.

assumptions.name: Area per anchor

assumptions.name: Not anchor design

flange-rating.edition: ASME B16.5 Pipe Flanges and Flanged Fittings pressure-temperature ratings, Material Group 1.1 (carbon steel, e.g. A105), by name. The ratings are read from the standard's table with linear interpolation.
flange-rating.freeAccess: The pressure-temperature rating is a fixed published table lookup; the Group 1.1 ratings are the standard's carbon-steel values, widely republished.
flange-rating.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
flange-rating.editionNote: The bundled ratings are MATERIAL GROUP 1.1 (carbon steel, e.g. A105); other material groups (stainless 2.x, low-alloy 1.x variants) have their OWN B16.5 tables. The value is the FLANGE'S rating - the weakest component (gasket, bolting, the mating pipe) can still govern the joint. A temperature outside the bundled 100 to 650 F range interpolates from the governing edition. The AHJ and the engineer of record govern.

assumptions.name: Material group
assumptions.value: bundled ratings are B16.5 Material Group 1.1 (carbon steel, e.g. A105); other groups have their own tables

assumptions.name: Interpolation
assumptions.value: linear between the table temperatures (100 to 650 F)

assumptions.name: Weakest component
assumptions.value: the flange rating is not the joint rating; gasket, bolting, and the mating pipe can govern

blowdown-heat-recovery.formula: blowdown / steam = feedwater TDS / (boiler TDS - feedwater TDS) = 1 / (cycles - 1); heat in blowdown = blowdown x (saturated liquid enthalpy at boiler pressure - makeup enthalpy); flash fraction = (h_f high - h_f low) / h_fg low; recovered = flash steam x (h_g low - h_makeup) + residual liquid x (h_f low - h_makeup) x exchanger effectiveness.
blowdown-heat-recovery.edition: The continuous surface blowdown mass balance and the flash relation by name -- the same TDS balance the blowdown-rate calculator uses, stated in cycles rather than in ppm, so the two do not disagree about how much blowdown a boiler makes. Saturated water enthalpies are entered from the steam tables. ASME, the boiler manufacturer, the water treatment program, and the jurisdiction's boiler inspector govern.
blowdown-heat-recovery.freeAccess: A mass and energy balance on figures the user enters from the steam tables; no chemistry limit is reproduced.
blowdown-heat-recovery.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
blowdown-heat-recovery.editionNote: Blowdown volume is set by chemistry, not by a valve position, so water treatment and blowdown rate are one decision. A plant at 5 cycles blows down 25% of its steam production; at 10 cycles it blows down 11%. The heat is what goes down the drain: 5,000 lb/hr at 150 psig carries about 310 BTU a pound above 60 degF makeup, 1.55 MMBTU an hour, roughly $140,000 a year of fuel at 80% efficiency and $9 per MMBTU over 8,000 hours. Recovery has two stages and both are worth taking, but treatment comes first because it removes the pounds rather than chasing their heat. The achievable cycles are set by the boiler water chemistry limits for the pressure and by the makeup quality; pushing past what the treatment program supports causes scale and carryover, which costs far more than the blowdown saved.

assumptions.name: Cycles are a chemistry limit
assumptions.value: not an optimization variable
assumptions.source: the water treatment program and the boiler manufacturer

assumptions.name: Surface blowdown only
assumptions.value: the intermittent bottom blowdown that removes sludge is separate
